column1: What is the fundamental architectural pattern underlying all interactive software systems like game loops?
column2: An event-driven state machine synchronized to a monotonic time source, transforming asynchronous external stimuli into a deterministic sequence of state transitions.

column1: Why can't a game loop advance simulation state using raw, variable wall-clock delta time?
column2: Minor variations in frame timing compound into divergent behavior—identical inputs applied to the same initial state produce different outcomes if processed with different timestep deltas, breaking determinism.

column1: Describe the fixed timestep integration with temporal accumulation pattern.
column2: Variable frame delta time is accumulated into a 'temporal debt' buffer, which is discharged in fixed-size quanta (e.g., 16.67ms for 60Hz). Leftover time rolls forward into the next frame, guaranteeing deterministic simulation at the cost of bounded input-to-effect latency.

column1: What three-phase cycle structures nearly all interactive real-time systems, from embedded firmware to MMO servers?
column2: 1) Input acquisition and event generation, 2) State transformation through discrete simulation steps, 3) Output rendering synchronized to display refresh.

column1: State the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) and its role in collision detection.
column2: Two convex polyhedra are disjoint if and only if there exists a separating axis along which their projections do not overlap. It transforms continuous collision detection into discrete scalar interval comparison tests.

column1: For 3D convex hull collision testing under SAT, what are the candidate separating axes?
column2: The face normals of both polyhedra, plus the cross products of all edge pairs between the two shapes.

column1: Why is naïve pairwise collision detection computationally intractable for large scenes, and how is this solved?
column2: Testing every object against every other yields O(n²) collision pairs. Spatial partitioning structures (BVH, spatial hash grids, sweep-and-prune) exploit spatial/temporal coherence to cull candidates down to typically O(n log n) or O(n).

column1: In an Entity Component System (ECS), define Entity, Component, and System.
column2: Entity: a unique integer ID with no behavior/data. Component: a plain data struct (e.g., Position, Health) stored contiguously by type. System: a function iterating over entities with a specific component signature to transform their data.

column1: Why does ECS outperform deep inheritance hierarchies for game object composition?
column2: Inheritance hierarchies explode combinatorially with new behavior combinations and scatter data via virtual dispatch, destroying cache locality. ECS stores same-type components contiguously, enabling CPU prefetching and SIMD-friendly iteration.

column1: What is the first invariant of networked multiplayer architecture regarding clock synchronization?
column2: No two clients can share the same wall-clock view of the world—this is a theorem following from the impossibility of perfectly synchronized clocks across distributed nodes, mitigated only by NTP approximations and logical clocks.

column1: What is the second invariant of networked multiplayer regarding input responsiveness, and what technique enforces it?
column2: Local responsiveness must never be held hostage to network RTT, since perceived input lag becomes noticeable above ~50–100ms. This is enforced via client-side prediction: speculatively applying player input locally and reconciling against server truth upon arrival.

column1: How do multiplayer games typically balance consistency vs. availability for different types of game state?
column2: Most state (e.g., positions) uses eventual consistency, allowing transient divergence that converges quickly. Non-idempotent state transitions (death, loot pickup, checkpoints) require strong consistency via authoritative server arbitration, even at the cost of latency.
